analysis.one_liner: Offers House candidates public campaign financing in exchange for running on small donations instead of large ones.
analysis.headline: The Fair Elections Now Act, which would have funded House campaigns with small donations and public money, died in the House Administration Committee with 70 cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a voluntary public financing system for House elections. Candidates who gather 1,500 small contributions ($5-$100) from state residents, totaling at least $50,000, could be certified as a "participating candidate" and receive a government payment plus a 500% match on small-dollar donations from their state — instead of raising money from large donors. Participating candidates would give up large contributions, personal spending, and joint fundraising committees, and would have to appear in public debates. The bill died in committee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, candidates who qualify could run competitive House campaigns funded by small donations from ordinary voters plus public funds, without seeking large contributions from wealthy donors, industry PACs, and lobbyists. Challengers benefit especially, since big donors give most of their money to incumbents. Taxpayers benefit only indirectly, if the bill's argument holds: that publicly financed candidates are less likely to steer legislation toward their major contributors.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Candidates who don't rely on big donors

how_it_helps.text: A candidate certified as a participant would receive fund allocations (40% of a base amount for a primary, 60% for a general) plus a 500% match on small-dollar donations from in-state residents, giving candidates money without large donors.

To qualify, a candidate must collect at least 1,500 (or 0.25% of the state's voting-age population, whichever is less) small contributions from state residents totaling $50,000, so only candidates with genuine local support can enter.
Participating candidates agree to accept no large contributions, spend no personal or family funds, take part in public debates, and remit unspent public money afterward.
The bill requires faster, electronic disclosure of campaign reports to the FEC (24-hour turnaround instead of 48), and bars participating candidates from joint fundraising committees.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, through appropriations to the Fair Elections Fund, plus voluntary contributions and half of FEC civil penalties. Participating candidates give up large contributions, personal wealth as a campaign source, and joint fundraising.

drawbacks.text: The program is funded by appropriations, meaning taxpayers would pay for candidates' campaigns even if they support candidates who refuse it.

Participating candidates could still benefit from party spending (subject to a reduced coordinated-spending cap) and would face outside groups' independent expenditures, which the bill cannot limit, so big money could still shape outcomes through those channels.
Candidates who participate give up most private fundraising and may end up with less money than well-funded opponents, a tradeoff many viable candidates would decline to make.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost to taxpayers would be roughly tens to a few hundred million dollars per cycle (a fraction of the base allocations paid only to candidates who win their seats' fund elections), against the bill's own argument that skewing toward large donors produces far larger regulatory and spending distortions [S3]. The main honest concerns are the efficiency of funding campaigns with tax dollars and the likelihood that unlimited outside spending would blunt the bill's effects. Against those is a program that ran entirely on volunteering by candidates and by small donors, which by design costs challengers less money and restores a cheaper path to office.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Administration Committee the day it was introduced and never came up again, dying quietly when the two-year Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 15, 2013 and referred to the House Committee on House Administration the same day.
The action history shows no further steps: no hearings, no markup, no vote, and the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
It drew 69 cosponsors (68 Democrats and 1 Republican) in addition to sponsor John Yarmuth.

The bill would have created a voluntary system in which House candidates who collect 1,500 small contributions (minimum $5) from state residents and $50,000 total could receive public funding and a 500% match on small-dollar donations instead of raising large private contributions.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large donors and the fundraising economy around House campaigns, who face no new competition from publicly financed candidates; members who rely on big contributions face no new pressure either.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action: no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Set the House agenda during the 113th Congress and did not schedule the bill for floor consideration.

sides.party_line_note: All 70 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats except one Republican (Rep. Walter Jones), and the Republican-held committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Large donors, lobbyists, and big-money bundlers
industries.note: Candidates who take the program give up large contributions, shrinking the pool of donors who can buy access. The bill's findings say the current system gives the wealthy disproportionate influence over the political process.

Candidates in the program would spend far less time and money on high-dollar fundraising, reducing billable fundraising and commission-based bundling (the bill bans paying per-qualifying-contribution commissions).

The bill sets its funding levels against historic campaign spending and media costs, treating expensive media advertising as a fixed cost of running for office rather than limiting it; ad spending continues to be the main vehicle for reaching voters.
The bill is voluntary, so members can keep the existing private-financing system; incumbents who fundraise most effectively could decline to participate and keep their advantage.
